Expert Consensus on Clinical Trials for Use of Systemic Therapy in Patients with Hepatocellular Carcinoma Undergoing Surgical and Locoregional Therapies
  • Source: Gut 2026;0:1–12. doi:10.1136/gutjnl-2026-339505
  • Topic: Clinical trial design for HCC systemic therapy in perioperative and combination settings
  • Author(s): Yarchoan M, Llovet JM, Kelley RK, et al. (27 experts from 24 institutions)
Background: HCC Burden and Treatment Landscape
  • HCC --> leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide
  • New cases and deaths projected to ↑ >75% by 2050 (if current rates unchanged)
  • Since 2020, immunotherapy-based combinations improved advanced-stage HCC outcomes
  • Median survival extended to ~2 years
  • 5-year survival now ~20% of patients
  • These advances create opportunities to investigate systemic therapy in earlier disease stages
Trial Design Challenges in HCC
  • Marked clinical and biological heterogeneity of early/intermediate-stage disease
  • Variability in tumour burden, distribution, cirrhosis coexistence
  • Potential difficulty assessing radiological response to ICIs
  • Variable assessment of surgical resectability across providers/centres
  • Prolonged OS in early/intermediate stages → trials need surrogate endpoints
  • Risk of reduced event rates and heavy right censoring with OS endpoints
Consensus Statements Overview
  • >70% approval threshold for consensus statements
  • 9 statements for neoadjuvant/perioperative therapy
  • 9 statements for combination locoregional + systemic therapy
Neoadjuvant/Perioperative Therapy Consensus
1.1 Prioritising Neoadjuvant Over Adjuvant Approaches
  • 93.3% agreement
  • Prioritise neoadjuvant or perioperative immunotherapy over adjuvant for early-stage HCC
  • Rationale: greater anticipated likelihood of benefit based on current evidence
  • Timing of immune priming is key → tumour antigens present to engage immune system
  • Tumour itself serves as in-situ vaccine
1.2 Insufficient Data on Perioperative Continuation
  • 93.3% agreement
  • No data to determine if continuation after surgery adds benefit over neoadjuvant alone
  • No specific approach favoured in current clinical trial design
1.3 Patient Population Criteria
  • 86.7% agreement
  • Include patients with tumours ≥5 cm
  • OR tumours ≥2 cm with at least one high-risk feature
High-Risk Features (defined)
  • Macrovascular invasion limited to subsegmental portal venous tumour thrombus (Vp1)
  • Serum AFP >400 ng/mL
  • Poor histological differentiation (when available)
  • Insufficient data to include other markers (DCP, imaging characteristics) at this time
  • Circulating cell-free DNA may serve as future high-risk feature
1.4 Optimal Treatment Duration
  • 80.0% agreement
  • Maximum duration: 12 weeks from cycle 1 day 1 to surgery
  • Rationale: minimise risk of disease progression leading to ineligibility for resection
  • Allow sufficient exposure for immune/antitumour effect
  • Median PFS with ICI therapy can be as short as 3–4 months
  • Median time to response across most trials shorter than 3 months
1.5 Anti-VEGF Timing Around Surgery
  • 93.3% agreement
  • For neoadjuvant approaches: discontinue anti-VEGF monoclonal antibodies ≥6 weeks before surgery
  • For perioperative strategies: do not resume anti-VEGF therapy until ≥6 weeks after surgery
1.6 Pretreatment Biopsy Recommendations
  • 86.7% agreement
  • Recommended for clinical trial protocols to facilitate translational research
  • Allows ruling out cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) or mixed HCC-CCA tumours
  • Should not be mandated if it would delay initiation of curative-intent therapy
  • Particularly for patients with characteristic imaging findings (LI-RADS criteria)
  • Traditional delay threshold: 3 months
1.7 Stratification Variables
  • 93.3% agreement
  • Randomise by:
  • Geographical region (captures variations in aetiology, cirrhosis, surgical approach)
  • Macrovascular invasion (Vp1 – segmental branches of portal vein)
  • Maximum tumour diameter >8 cm
  • Serum AFP level >400 ng/mL
1.8 Primary Endpoint Recommendation
  • 100% agreement
  • 2-year event-free survival (EFS)
  • Use restricted mean survival time for assessment
  • EFS captures: failure to undergo surgery (progression/treatment-related toxicities), recurrence after surgery, death from any cause
  • 2-year landmark selected because goal is reducing early recurrence (micrometastatic disease)
  • Does not impact late recurrence (de novo tumours)
1.9 Key Secondary Endpoints
  • 100% agreement
  • Safety (treatment-related adverse events)
  • Long-term overall survival (OS)
  • Major pathological response (MPR) – defined as ≥70% tumour necrosis
  • Recent data suggests ≥90% tumour necrosis may better predict RFS
  • Radiographic response (per RECIST criteria)
  • Note: radiographic response may underestimate MPR in up to 1/3 of cases
  • Time to recurrence (TTR)
  • Health-related quality of life (patient-reported outcomes)
Combination Locoregional + Systemic Therapy Consensus
2.1 Comparison Arms Based on Tumour Burden
  • 86.7% agreement (both statements)
  • Limited intrahepatic tumour burden → compare combination therapy vs locoregional therapy alone
  • Larger intrahepatic tumour burden or locally advanced HCC → compare combination therapy vs immunotherapy alone
2.2 Trial Population for Combination vs LRT
  • 93.3% agreement
  • Intermediate-stage HCC (BCLC stage B) eligible for locoregional therapy
  • Early-stage patients with at least one high-risk feature (not amenable to curative therapy)
High-Risk Features for Early-Stage Inclusion
  • AFP levels >400 ng/mL
  • Tumour size >5 cm
  • Imaging features: disrupted capsule or infiltrative morphology
2.3 Trial Population for Combination vs Systemic Therapy
  • 93.3% agreement
  • Intermediate-stage HCC deemed suboptimal for locoregional therapy alone
  • Patients with limited vascular invasion (Vp1-Vp2 – segmental or second-order portal vein branches)
2.4 Liver Function and Performance Status
  • 93.3% agreement
  • Both trial populations restricted to:
  • Child-Pugh class A liver function
  • ECOG performance status 0–1
  • Rationale: reduce confounding from liver dysfunction
2.5 Control Arm Selection
  • 93.3% agreement
  • Globally: TACE is recommended control arm for trials comparing combination vs locoregional therapy
  • USA: TARE is more relevant control arm (many centres now use TARE instead of TACE)
  • Technical parameters should specify: catheter selectivity levels, type of administration (DEB-TACE vs conventional TACE)
2.6 Stratification Factors
  • 100% agreement
  • Randomise by:
  • Tumour burden (prior trials used up-to-7 criteria or 6-and-12 criteria)
  • Liver dysfunction assessed by ALBI grade
  • Baseline AFP level >400 ng/mL
  • Note: both criteria fail to capture nuances of tumour distribution and liver segments involved
2.7 Primary Endpoints
  • 100% agreement
  • Dual primary endpoints: PFS and OS
  • Use alpha-recycling strategy for statistical significance
  • Significant PFS improvement + sufficient signal toward OS benefit (HR ~0.8 vs control) needed for clinical adoption
2.8 Key Secondary Endpoints
  • 100% agreement
  • Safety
  • Objective response rate (ORR)
  • Depth of response
  • Health-related quality of life
  • Downstaging to surgical therapy (measure by change in tumour burden, not therapeutic intent)
  • Time to liver function deterioration
  • Time to progression (TTP)
Evidence Supporting Combination Therapy Trials
3.1 Recent Phase III RCT Results
  • EMERALD-1: durvalumab + bevacizumab following TACE → improved PFS (HR 0.77; 95% CI 0.61–0.98)
  • LEAP-012: lenvatinib + pembrolizumab + TACE → improved PFS (HR 0.66; 95% CI 0.51–0.84)
  • TALENTACE: novel endpoint TACE-PFS (HR 0.71; 95% CI 0.55–0.92)
  • None demonstrated OS improvement
3.2 Trial Population Heterogeneity Issues
  • LEAP-012: advanced stages included in 9% of patients
  • EMERALD-1: advanced stages in 17%
  • TALENTACE: advanced stages in 21%
  • Over half of EMERALD-1 patients exceeded up-to-7 criteria
  • Nearly 50% of LEAP-012 had tumour burden score >6
3.3 Patients Unsuitable for Locoregional Therapy
  • Extensive bilobar disease (>50% liver involvement)
  • Infiltrative growth patterns
  • High risk of liver dysfunction after locoregional therapies
  • Retrospective analysis: upfront systemic therapy showed better PFS vs TACE (median 16.0 vs 3.0 months) for patients beyond up-to-7 criteria
Statistical Considerations
  • Primary endpoints should use methods robust to non-proportional hazards
  • Restricted mean survival time
  • Weighted log-rank tests
  • Extensive evaluation of operating characteristics recommended
  • Assess power, type I error, robustness under realistic assumptions
  • Multiple primary endpoints: use gatekeeping or alpha-switching strategies for family-wise error control
Adaptive Trial Design Considerations
  • Group-sequential designs
  • Bayesian sequential go/no-go monitoring
  • Response-adaptive randomisation
  • Adaptive enrichment
  • Master protocols (basket, umbrella, platform trials)
  • Bayesian hierarchical models for partial borrowing across geographical regions
Future Research Directions
  • Collect human biological material: serial blood collections and tissue at index visit
  • Enable molecular subtyping for biomarker-driven patient selection
  • Identify immune microenvironment signatures predictive of immunotherapy response
  • Develop resistance mechanisms elucidating combination synergy
  • Detailed granular radiology data (number, size, distribution, degree of liver involvement, vascular invasion)
  • Multimodal AI-based algorithms with blood-based biomarkers and clinical data
Figures
Figure 1: Proposed randomised clinical trial schema for patients with early-stage hepatocellular carcinoma at high risk of recurrence following resection. Eligible patients include those with tumours ≥5 cm or tumours ≥2 cm with at least one high-risk feature, including AFP >200 ng/mL, poor histological differentiation or limited macrovascular invasion (Vp1). Patients are randomised to either standard-of-care upfront surgical resection or neoadjuvant systemic therapy followed by surgical resection within 12 weeks of C1D1. Randomisation is stratified by geographical region, presence of Vp1 macrovascular invasion, maximum tumour diameter >8 cm and AFP >400 ng/mL. The primary endpoint is 2 year event-free survival assessed using restricted mean survival time. Key secondary endpoints include major pathological response, radiographic response, time to recurrence, safety and overall survival. In this illustrative schema incorporating bevacizumab and ICI, bevacizumab is administered only at C1D1 and then withheld to allow an adequate washout period prior to surgery, mitigating perioperative bleeding and wound-healing risks. The optimal washout interval may vary depending on the half-life and pharmacological properties of the specific agent utilised. AFP, alpha-fetoprotein; C1D1, cycle 1 day 1; ICI, immune checkpoint inhibitor; Vp1, vascular invasion into segmental branches of the portal vein.
Figure 2: Proposed randomised clinical trial schemes for patients with intermediate-stage HCC. (A) Clinical trials evaluating combination therapy versus LRT alone should include patients with intermediate-stage HCC who are eligible for LRT and selected patients with early-stage HCC who are not amenable to curative therapy and possess at least one high-risk feature. Eligible patients should have Child-Pugh A liver function and ECOG performance status 0–1. Patients are randomised to receive standard-of-care LRT alone or combination systemic therapy plus LRT. Randomisation should incorporate stratification by tumour burden, liver dysfunction as assessed by ALBI grade, baseline AFP level and geographical region. The co-primary endpoints are PFS and OS using an alpha-recycling strategy. Key secondary endpoints include safety, objective response rate, depth of response, health-related quality of life, downstaging, time to liver function deterioration and TTP. (B) Clinical trials evaluating combination therapy versus systemic therapy alone should include patients with intermediate-stage HCC who are considered suboptimal candidates for LRT alone because of larger intrahepatic tumour burden, as well as patients with limited vascular invasion (Vp1-2). Eligible patients should have Child-Pugh A liver function and ECOG performance status 0–1. Patients are randomised to receive standard-of-care systemic therapy alone or systemic therapy alone with LRT. Randomisation should incorporate stratification by tumour burden, liver dysfunction as assessed by ALBI grade, baseline AFP level and geographical region. The co-primary endpoints are PFS and OS using an alpha-recycling strategy. Key secondary endpoints include safety, objective response rate, depth of response, health-related quality of life, downstaging, time to liver function deterioration and TTP. alpha-AFP, alpha-fetoprotein; ALBI, Albumin-Bilirubin; ECOG, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group; HCC, hepatocellular carcinoma; LRT, locoregional therapy; SOC, standard of care; TACE, transarterial chemoembolisation; TARE, transarterial radioembolisation; Vp1-2, vascular invasion into segmental or second-order branches of the portal vein.
